title: Why do bulk @Query UPDATE and DELETE statements need @Modifying and @Transactional? What do clearAutomatically and flushAutomatically do, and how do they prevent a stale persistence context?

s1_definition.profdef: In Spring Data JPA, a custom `@Query` that performs an UPDATE or DELETE must be annotated with `@Modifying` so Spring knows to call `executeUpdate` instead of expecting a result set, and it must run inside a transaction, so you add `@Transactional`. A bulk modifying query runs directly against the database and bypasses the persistence context, so entities already loaded into the first-level cache can become stale. The `flushAutomatically` attribute flushes pending changes to the database before the query runs, and the `clearAutomatically` attribute clears the persistence context after the query runs so that subsequent reads fetch fresh data from the database.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a clerk at the National Bank of India has photocopies of several account pages on his desk (the persistence context). Now the manager issues a bulk order: "add one percent interest to every savings account" straight into the master ledger (a bulk UPDATE). The clerk's photocopies are now out of date because they still show the old balances. `flushAutomatically` makes the clerk first write any pending edits into the master ledger before the bulk order runs, and `clearAutomatically` makes the clerk throw away his stale photocopies after the bulk order so that next time he needs an account he fetches a fresh page from the master ledger.
s1_definition.oneliner: Bulk UPDATE/DELETE queries skip the persistence context, so use `@Modifying` with `@Transactional` and set `clearAutomatically = true` to avoid reading stale cached entities afterward.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** In Spring Data JPA, a custom `@Query` that performs an UPDATE or DELETE must be annotated with `@Modifying` so Spring knows to call `executeUpdate` instead of expecting a result set, and it must run inside a transaction, so you add `@Transactional`. A bulk modifying query runs directly against the database and bypasses the persistence context, so entities already loaded into the first-level cache can become stale. The `flushAutomatically` attribute flushes pending changes to the database before the query runs, and the `clearAutomatically` attribute clears the persistence context after the query runs so that subsequent reads fetch fresh data from the database.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine a clerk at the National Bank of India has photocopies of several account pages on his desk (the persistence context). Now the manager issues a bulk order: "add one percent interest to every savings account" straight into the master ledger (a bulk UPDATE). The clerk's photocopies are now out of date because they still show the old balances. `flushAutomatically` makes the clerk first write any pending edits into the master ledger before the bulk order runs, and `clearAutomatically` makes the clerk throw away his stale photocopies after the bulk order so that next time he needs an account he fetches a fresh page from the master ledger.

**One line to remember:** Bulk UPDATE/DELETE queries skip the persistence context, so use `@Modifying` with `@Transactional` and set `clearAutomatically = true` to avoid reading stale cached entities afterward.

sections.s2_technical:
A normal derived query or a `@Query` with a SELECT returns data. But when your JPQL is an UPDATE or DELETE, Spring Data cannot treat it the same way. You must add `@Modifying` so Spring calls `Query.executeUpdate()`, which returns the number of affected rows instead of a list. For example `@Modifying @Query("UPDATE Account a SET a.balance = a.balance + :interest WHERE a.type = 'SAVINGS'") int applyInterest(@Param("interest") BigDecimal interest);` returns how many accounts were updated.

A modifying query changes data, so it must run in a transaction. If there is no active transaction you get a `TransactionRequiredException`. You can put `@Transactional` on the repository method, but the cleaner and more common practice is to put it on the service method that calls the repository, so the whole business operation is one transaction. For example the service method `applyMonthlyInterest` is annotated `@Transactional` and calls the modifying repository method inside it.

The crucial point is that a bulk modifying query runs directly as SQL against the database and completely bypasses the persistence context, also called the first-level cache. Hibernate does not know which in-memory entities the bulk statement affected. So if you already loaded Rajesh's account into the persistence context and then run a bulk UPDATE that changes his balance in the database, the in-memory copy still shows the old balance. Reading it again in the same transaction returns the stale cached value, not the new database value. This is the stale persistence context problem.

The `clearAutomatically` attribute solves this. When set to true, Spring clears the persistence context after the modifying query runs, so Hibernate forgets all the entities it had cached. The next time you load any entity, Hibernate goes back to the database and gets fresh data. For example `@Modifying(clearAutomatically = true) @Query("UPDATE Account a SET a.status = 'FROZEN' WHERE a.balance < 0") int freezeOverdrawn();` ensures that after the freeze, any account you read reflects the new status. The default is false, which is why people get confused when their reads after a bulk update show old values.

The `flushAutomatically` attribute handles the other direction. When set to true, Spring flushes any pending changes in the persistence context to the database before the modifying query runs. This matters when you have made in-memory changes that have not been written yet, and your bulk query depends on them. For example if you changed some accounts' types in memory and then run a bulk UPDATE that filters by type, you want those pending changes flushed first so the bulk query sees them. The default is false, so by default Hibernate does not force a flush before the bulk statement, which can cause the bulk query to run against data that does not yet reflect your pending changes.

A senior-level nuance is that the right combination for most bulk operations is `@Modifying(clearAutomatically = true, flushAutomatically = true)` plus `@Transactional`. Flush first so the database reflects pending work, run the bulk statement, then clear so later reads are fresh. Another nuance is that bulk UPDATE and DELETE statements do not cascade and do not trigger entity lifecycle callbacks or optimistic locking version increments, because they bypass the entity layer entirely. So if you have `@Version` optimistic locking or `@PreUpdate` callbacks, a bulk statement will not honor them, which is a deliberate tradeoff you accept for performance on large updates. For small numbers of entities you would load and modify them normally so lifecycle and versioning work; for millions of rows you use a bulk modifying query for speed.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, interest must be applied to every savings account at month end. There could be millions of accounts. Loading each one into memory, adding interest, and saving it back would be painfully slow and use huge memory. This is exactly why we use a bulk `@Query` UPDATE with `@Modifying` — one SQL statement updates all savings accounts at once.

Problem 2 — A developer loaded Rajesh's account earlier in the same transaction, then ran the bulk interest update, then read Rajesh's balance again and saw the old value without the interest. This is exactly the stale persistence context problem, and `clearAutomatically = true` fixes it by clearing the cache so the re-read fetches the new balance from the database.

Problem 3 — Before applying interest, some accounts had their type changed to SAVINGS in memory but not yet flushed. The bulk update filters by type SAVINGS, so it would miss those accounts. This is exactly what `flushAutomatically = true` fixes by flushing pending changes to the database before the bulk update runs.

What the code will do. The `Account` entity has id, holderName, type, and balance. The `AccountRepository` has a bulk `applyInterest` modifying query with both flush and clear set to true. The `InterestService` is transactional, demonstrates loading Rajesh before the bulk update, runs the update, and reads Rajesh again to prove the value is now fresh. The demo shows the stale read problem avoided and the correct final balances.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a 1 percent monthly interest rate. Rajesh (SAV2001) is a savings account with Rs.1,000,000. Priya (CUR3001) is a current account with Rs.250,000, which should not get interest.

Step 1. The transactional service method starts. It loads Rajesh's account by id. Hibernate puts a copy into the persistence context showing the balance of Rs.1,000,000. The log confirms the cached before-value.

Step 2. The service calls the repository's modifying query. Because flushAutomatically is true, Hibernate first flushes any pending changes to the database so the bulk statement sees the latest committed state.

Step 3. The bulk UPDATE runs directly as SQL. It adds 1 percent to every savings account's balance in the database. Rajesh's database row is now Rs.1,010,000. Priya is a current account, so her row is untouched at Rs.250,000. This statement bypasses the persistence context entirely, so the in-memory copy of Rajesh still says Rs.1,000,000.

Step 4. Because clearAutomatically is true, Hibernate clears the persistence context after the bulk update. The stale copy of Rajesh is discarded.

Step 5. The service reads Rajesh again. Since the cache was cleared, Hibernate fetches a fresh row from the database and returns Rs.1,010,000, the correct new value. Without clearAutomatically, this read would have returned the stale Rs.1,000,000.

```

2026-10-23 16:20:01 [FINE   ] FLUSH: pending changes written to DB

    │
    ▼
  InterestService.applyMonthlyInterest()  @Transactional
    │
    │ repo.findById("SAV2001")
    ▼
  Persistence Context (cache)
    │  SAV2001 copy = 1,000,000   (loaded)
    │
    │ repo.applyInterest(0.01)  @Modifying(flush=true, clear=true)
    ├─ flushAutomatically → write pending changes to DB
    ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ DB: bulk UPDATE SAVINGS       │   bypasses cache
  │ SAV2001: 1,000,000 → 1,010,000│
  │ CUR3001: 250,000 (untouched)  │
  └──────────────┬────────────────┘
                 │ clearAutomatically → empty the cache

  Persistence Context now EMPTY
    │  repo.findById("SAV2001") → MISS → load FRESH from DB
    ▼
  Rajesh = 1,010,000 (correct, not stale)   Priya = 250,000

  WITHOUT clearAutomatically: re-read returns STALE 1,000,000
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
When I write a custom query in Spring Data JPA that performs an UPDATE or DELETE instead of a SELECT, I must add the Modifying annotation so Spring calls executeUpdate and returns the affected row count rather than expecting a result set. Because it changes data, it must run inside a transaction, so I put the Transactional annotation on the service method that drives the operation, otherwise I get a TransactionRequiredException.

The subtle part that interviewers probe is cache coherence. A bulk modifying query runs directly as SQL against the database and completely bypasses the persistence context, the first-level cache. So if I already loaded an entity into memory and then run a bulk update that changes it in the database, the in-memory copy is now stale, and reading it again in the same transaction returns the old value. In my banking project this bit us during the month-end interest batch. We loaded Rajesh's savings account, ran a bulk update that added one percent interest to every savings account, then read his balance again and saw the old amount because the cached copy was never updated.

The fix is the two attributes on the Modifying annotation. clearAutomatically set to true clears the persistence context after the bulk query runs, so the next read of any entity fetches fresh data from the database instead of a stale cached copy. flushAutomatically set to true flushes any pending in-memory changes to the database before the bulk query runs, so the bulk statement operates on the latest state. For almost every bulk operation I use both together along with the Transactional annotation: flush first, run the bulk statement, then clear.

The last thing I always mention is the tradeoff. Because bulk statements bypass the entity layer, they do not cascade to related entities, they do not trigger lifecycle callbacks like PreUpdate, and they do not increment optimistic locking versions. That is the deliberate price for being able to update millions of rows in one fast SQL statement. For a handful of entities I would load and modify them normally so versioning and callbacks work, but for a huge batch like applying interest to every savings account, the bulk modifying query with clear and flush enabled is the right tool.

---

keyPoints: Must have @Transactional — write queries need a transaction
clearAutomatically=true: clear persistence context after update
Without @Modifying: Spring treats UPDATE query as SELECT — fails
